senses.gloss:
anuvāka
(‘saying after’)
------------------------------------------
Literally the word means ‘reciting’ (the वेदस्) ‘after’ or ‘following’ the teacher. Hence it refers to the recitation of the वेदस् in general. However, it is used in a more technical sense, to indicate a division of the Vedic mantras.
The Ṛgveda Saṁhitā, the basic scripture of हिन्दुइस्म्, is divided into ten books each of which is called ‘maṇḍala.’ Each मण्डल is again divided into several subsections called anuvākas. The anuvākas are further subdivided into sūktas, each सूक्त containing one or more ṛks (verses). There are 85 anuvākas in the Ṛgveda.
Śaunaka has prepared an index for these anuvākas, known as Anuvākānu-kramaṇī.

anumāna
(‘to measure or draw conclusions, following [a given premise]’ )
------------------------------------------
Indian systems of philosophy have paid considerable attention to the problem of knowledge and the means of obtaining it. The object to be known is called ‘prameya’ (‘that which is measured or known’), the means of knowing it is ‘pramāṇa’ (‘the measure’) and the know-ledge obtained thus is ‘pramā’ (‘that which is measured’).
The प्रमाणस् accepted by the various schools vary from two to six. However, almost all the theistic schools are agreed on three of them and consider them as more basic. They are: प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception), अनुमान (inference) and āptavākya (testimony), the āgama or scriptural testimony being considered the highest in the last category.
When smoke is seen on a distant hill, though fire itself is not seen directly, we conclude that there is fire on the hill since smoke is invariably associated with fire. Here, the means of our know-ledge of fire on the hill is ‘anumāna’ or inference. We are measuring (mā = to measure) or knowing the object of know-ledge (fire), following (anu = to follow) a given premise (i.e., the smoke and the invariable concomitance of smoke with fire known to exist from our earlier experiences).
Some technical terms commonly used while defining अनुमान are: ‘sādhya’ (what is to be proved; here, the fire), ‘hetu’ (the cause for such inference; here, smoke) and ‘pakṣa’ (that which takes a side, or causes doubts; here, the hill).
See also PRAMĀṆAS.

anuloma
(‘with the hair or grain’)
------------------------------------------
Anything that is the prescribed or accepted order is termed ‘anuloma’ as opposed to ‘pratiloma’ (‘opposed to the hair or grain’) which indicates the reverse order. The word is widely used with regard to marriages and castes. An अनुलोम मर्रिअगे is one in which the male is of a higher caste than the female. Offsprings of such unions belong to a set of castes called अनुलोम castes.
In the प्रतिलोम मर्रिअगे the male is of a lower caste than the female and the offsprings belong to प्रतिलोम castes.

anubandha-catuṣṭaya
(‘four-fold connection’)
------------------------------------------
Works on Advaita Vedānta usually commence with the description of the anunbandha-catuṣṭaya. Anubandha is that which connects or binds, the factors which bind the entire system together into a connected whole. There are four such factors and hence the word ‘catuṣṭaya’ (a group of four).
The first anubandha is ‘adhikārin,’ the person competent to study and practise the science. The second is ‘viṣaya,’ the subject matter dealt with in the treatise. The third is ‘prayojana,’ utility to be gained by its study and practice. The last is ‘sambandha’ or connection, usually between the book that purports to deal with the science and the science itself, or, between the work and the utility promised.
Though this is used as a ‘technical word’ in Advaita literature, it is a general concept that can be applied to other fields of knowledge also.

anūbandhyā
(‘bound, following [the sacrifice]’)
------------------------------------------
Towards the end of the अग्निष्टोम sacrifice, after the udayanīya rite, a barren cow used to be immolated and sacrificed to the gods मित्र and वरुण. This cow was called anu(ū)bandhyā. Sometimes three barren cows used to be sacrificed to Mitrā-वरुण, विश्वेदेवस् and बृहस्पति, as in वाजपेय, राजसूय and Sattra yāgas. Substitutes of pāyasam (pudding) and आमिक्षा (curdled milk) have also been mentioned, even in the earlier works. Sacrifice of these cows has been given up long since.
See also AGNIṢṬOMA, RĀJASŪYA, UDAYANĪYA and VĀJAPEYA.

anuvākyā
(‘to say after’)
------------------------------------------
Performance of Vedic rites involves several complex processes. Appropriate Vedic hymns selected from the various sections of the वेदस् (mostly from the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā) have to be chanted or sung at certain specified stages during these rites. Such hymns are categorized as याज्या, अनुवाक्या, शस्त्र and so on.
The अनुवाक्या hymns—also called puronuvākyā—are to be chanted by the होतृ (priest reciting the ṛks) when the अध्वर्यु (priest following the Yajurveda) cuts the पुरोडाश (cakes for offering) into several parts. They are actually invitations to the respective deities to accept the offerings allotted to them. Since the name of the particular deity appears in the first part of the hymn, the hymn itself is also called पुरोनुवाक्या (puras = first, in front). For instance, Ṛgveda 8.44.12 and 1.91.11 are used as anuvākyās.
See also YĀJYĀ and ŚASTRA.

anuyāja
(‘after-offering’)
------------------------------------------
Among the few sacrifices that an आहिताग्नि (one who has ceremonially kindled the Vedic fires) is expected to perform regularly, Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa should specially be mentioned. They belong to the class called ‘iṣṭi’ (needing four priests) and are performed on the new-मोओन् day and full-मोओन् day respectively.
During these sacrifices, certain minor offerings are made before and after the principal offerings. Such offerings made before the principal ones are called prayājas (pra = before) and those made after the principal ones are termed anuyājas (anu = after).
The prayājas are oblations of आज्य (clarified butter or ghee) and are five in number, addressed to deities like samidhaḥ, narāśaṁsa and others.
The anuyājas are only three and offered to बर्हिस्, narāśaṁsa and अग्नि sviṣṭakṛt.
The word is sometimes spelled as anūyāja also.
See also DARŚA-PŪRṆAMĀSA.

anupātaka
(‘secondary sin’)
------------------------------------------
Human beings are generally prone to commit sins due to certain basic weaknesses inherent in the psycho-physical system. For instance, hunger and sex or passions and prejudices. When they are not sublimated or controlled or not let out through outlets approved by धर्म (righteousness or religious laws) sin will result. A sin is generally termed ‘pātaka,’ that which makes one fall (pat = to fall), from the ideal.
The smṛtis and धर्मशास्त्रस् have categorised the sins in various ways. अनुपातक is one such, considered less than mahāpātaka (grievous sin) but in effect almost approaches it. False accusations against one’s गुरु (father or preceptor) and sexual relationship with women like the wife of a learned ब्राह्मण or those seeking one’s protection are two such sins.
A sin must be expiated. Various kinds of expiations known as prāyaścittas are prescribed for the various crimes. As regards the anupātakas, the prāyaścittas are almost the same as the ones prescribed for the महापातकस्. Performing Aśva-medha sacrifice and visiting places of पिल्ग्रिमगे are prominently mentioned in this list of prāyaścittas for the anupātakas.
See also PĀTAKA and PRĀYAŚCITTA.

Anuvyākhyāna
------------------------------------------
The वेदान्त दर्शन, considered to be the crown-jewel of all the Hindu philosophical systems, is based on the three basic works known as ‘prasthāna-traya.’ प्रस्थानत्रय comprises the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahmasūtras and the Bhagavadgītā. Any philosophical or reli-gious system, to be acceptable to the Hindu tradition, had to acknowledge the authority of these three works, or at least, not contradict them.
Of these three works, the Brahma-sūtras, also known as the Vedāntasūtras or Śārīrakasūtras, is a compendium of Upaniṣadic thoughts presented in a syste-matic manner. Since the sūtras (aphorisms) of this work are as enigmatic as they are laconic, several sages and savants have tried to expound their true meaning and purport through erudite commentaries.
One of the more important savants who have composed such commentaries on the Brahmasūtras is मध्वाचार्य (A. D. 1197—1276) also known as Ānandatīrtha. He is the first acārya (teacher) to syste-matize the द्वैत school of Vedānta, based on the प्रस्थानत्रय.
Madhvācārya is reputed to have composed four commentaries on the Brahmasūtras: Brahmasūtra Bhāṣya, Anuvyākhyāna, Nyāyavivaraṇa and Aṇubhāṣya.
It is said that Anuvyākhyāna, the second work, was composed by Madhvā-cārya at the instance of त्रिविक्रम Paṇḍita, one of his more important disciples, who was not satisfied with the Bhāṣya since it was not sufficiently polemical.
The Anuvyākhyāna, a metrical master-piece in 900 verses is a highly polemical work which subjects all other schools of interpretation opposed to the द्वैत system to a ruthlessly critical examination. The most celebrated work of जयतीर्थ (A. D. 1345-1388), the Nyāya-sudhā, is actually a commentary on the Anuvyākhyāna. The work closely follows the Brahmasūtras, chapter by chapter, in its essential logical position.
The more important topics discussed may be briefly summed up as follows: ओङ्कार is the designation of ब्रह्मन् and the purport of the वेदस्; God is supremely independent and the whole च्रेअतिओन् depends upon Him; all bondage is real; the universe is real; but emancipation is possible by the grace of God.
The work devotes a major part to the criticism of Advaita Vedānta.
See also BRAHMASŪTRAS, DVAITA-VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA, JAYATĪRTHA and MADHVĀCĀRYA.

anugraha-mūrti
(‘icon showing favour’)
------------------------------------------
Temples and इमगे wओर्स्हिप् have had a long history in Hindu religion and culture. Each of the three main cults of हिन्दुइस्म्, viz., शैविस्म्, शाक्तैस्म् and वैष्णविस्म् has given rise to a variety of icons during the course of its evolution. One set of such icons pertaining especially to Lord शिव, showing benediction to his devotees is called ‘anugraha-mūrti.’
Iconographical works record six such anugrahamūrtis, mūrtis or icons showing anugraha or benediction to Caṇḍeśa (one of the attendants of शिव), Nandīśvara (Śiva’s mount), विष्णु, Vighneśvara or गणेश, अर्जुन (the Pāṇḍava hero) and रावण (the demon king of लङ्का). One hand of the image is usually kept on the head of the supplicant while one of the other hands exhibits abhayamudrā (protec-tion—giving pose) or varadamudrā (boon-giving pose).

anupalabdhi
(‘non-perception’)
------------------------------------------
Out of the six प्रमाणस् (means of obtaining knowledge) accepted by the (Bhāṭṭa) Mīmāṁsā and the Advaita Vedānta systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, अनुपलब्धि or non-perception forms the last. It is one of the five sources of non-perceptual knowledge.
According to the Mīmāṁsā epistemo-logy of कुमारिल भट्ट, the non-perception of an object is a source of our immediate चोग्नितिओन् of the non-existence (abhāva) of that object. For instance, how is the non-existence of a jar on the table in front of us, known? It is known from the absence of its चोग्नितिओन्, since, being a negative fact, it cannot be perceived through the senses.
Can we not get this knowledge through अनुमान or inference? Why should we accept an additional source of knowledge? No, we cannot; because there is no concomitant relationship between non-perception and non-existence, as for instance in the case of non-perception in the dark. Hence अनुपलब्धि as an additional means of knowledge must be accepted. However, it is to be noted that if a thing would have been perceived under given circumstances, but not perceived, then only its अनुपलब्धि or non-perception becomes a proof of its non-existence. Such अनुपलब्धि is sometimes called ‘yogyānupalabdhi.’
See also PRAMĀṆAS.

anustaraṇī
(‘[a] secondary [animal] that is spread over’)
------------------------------------------
An old cow which is set free during the ड़ुनेरल् रितेस् and which is believed to help the deceased to cross the वैतरणी (a fetid river between the earth and नरक or the nether world) is technically called अनुस्तरणी.
Since the root ‘stṛ’ has the sense of ‘spreading,’ अनुस्तरणी may also refer to an old cow which is immolated during the ड़ुनेरल् रितेस्, dissected and its various limbs spread on the dead body. This practice, however, ceased to exist long back.
The अनुस्तरणी is sometimes called rājagavī also.
See also ANTYEṢṬI.

anuśaya
(‘left over [even] after [experience]’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism believes in the theory of कर्म (actions) and पुनर्जन्म (reincarnation). As a result of पुण्य (meritorious deeds), the जीव (the individual) is said to go to svargaloka (heaven) or candraloka (the lunar world) and return to the earth after the merit is used up. Even after this पुण्य is exhausted, there are other karmas still left over, which will fructify and give the जीव further births and experiences. Such residual कर्म is called अनुशय.
The word is sometimes used in the sense of पश्चात्-ताप or repentance.
See also PRĀRABDHA-KARMA.

anudātta
(‘not raised’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedic Saṁhitās have been preserved for millennia due to the well-orga-nized system of ‘svaras’ or intonations. Such svaras are of three types: उदात्त, अनुदात्त and स्वरित. They are generally translated as ‘raised,’ ‘not raised’ and ‘falling.’ They are musical in nature.
The अनुदात्त is indicated by a horizontal line below the letter, the उदात्त without any sign and the स्वरित with a vertical line above the letter. For instance: Oṁ saha nā̍āvavatu. Here ‘sa’ is an अनुदात्त and ‘n̍a’ is a स्वरित. The other letters are all उदात्त.
While chanting, the उदात्त letters are chanted as the basic note (‘sa’ or ṣaḍja of मुसिच्), the अनुदात्त as one note below (‘ni’ or निषाद) and the स्वरित as one note above (‘ri’ or ऋषभ).

Anuśāsana-parva
------------------------------------------
Also called Ānuśāsanika-parva, this is the thirteenth book of the great epic Mahābhārata containing lengthy expositions on धर्म. For details, See MAHĀ-BHĀRATA.

Anumati
(‘approval’)
------------------------------------------
There are several वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् performed on different days, determined by the phases of the मोओन्. The मोओन् rising on the 15th day of the bright fortnight, which is still associated with the 14th day (caturdaśī), will have one कला or digit less. It is said that iṣṭis (sacrifices) performed on that day are received favourably by the gods and manes. In Vedic literature the day itself is personified as the goddess अनुमति. She is to be propitiated with oblations at a certain stage during the राजसूय sacrifice.
See also RĀJASŪYA.

Anugītā
(‘following the ’)
------------------------------------------
The immense popularity of the Bhagavadgītā—generally known as the Gītā—inspired a number of authors of didactic literature to produce more such works. Most of these are imitations and are almost always incorporated into bigger works like the epics and the पुराणस्. There are as many as thirty six such gītās, out of which sixteen are from the Mahābhārata alone. Anugītā is one such and perhaps better known than the others. The name ‘Anugītā’ is derived from the fact that it purports to follow (anu = following) the Gītā.
The Anugītā comprises chapters 16-51 of the fourteenth book (Āśvamedhikaparva) of the Mahābhārata and is in the form of a dialogue between Śrī कृष्ण and अर्जुन. Being eager to recapitulate the teachings of the Bhagavadgītā, अर्जुन requests Śrī कृष्ण for the same. After taking अर्जुन to task for having forgotten the teaching so soon and confessing that he is not in a high state of योग now, Śrī कृष्ण gives him another set of teachings, mostly by reciting stories and dialogues that took place between sages of yore.
The topics dealt with in this गीता can be briefly indicated as follows: the travels and travails of the जीव or the individual सोउल्, कर्म and rebirth, means of attaining मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, jñānayajña or knowledge compared to a sacrifice, a description of the prāṇas or vital airs, the greatness of the अन्तर्यामिन् or the inner controller, spiritual experience described with the allegory of a forest, story of परशुराम, description of the three guṇas and their effects, च्रेअतिओन्, greatness of spiritual wisdom, duties of people in the four āśramas, individual and Supreme selves, nature of austerity, nature of आत्मन् or Self.
The section comprising the chapters 20-34 is called Brāhmaṇagītā since it was taught by an enlightened ब्राह्मण to his wife.

anuvyavasāya
(‘after-चोग्नितिओन्’)
------------------------------------------
Indian philosophical systems, called darśanas, have analyzed the phenomenon of knowledge in all its aspects. Out of the several प्रमाणस् or means of knowledge, प्रत्यक्ष or direct perception is universally accepted and placed as the first in the series.
When a pot is seen by the eyes and the knowledge ’This is a pot‘ arises in the मिन्द्, such a knowledge is called vyavasāya or determinate चोग्नितिओन्. However, this is immediately followed by another knowledge ‘I know this pot’ thus relating the earlier knowledge to the self. Since this vyavasāya or चोग्नितिओन् rises after the first, it is termed ‘anuvyavasāya’ (anu = after).
This is a later doctrine developed by the न्याय school.
See also PRAMĀṆAS.

Anūrādhā
(‘causing welfare’)
------------------------------------------
Anūrādhā (also ‘Anurādhā’) is the 17th of the 27 nakṣatras or constellations of स्तर्स् listed in Hindu अस्त्रोनोम्य्. The स्तर्स् comprising this नक्षत्र are beta, delta and pi Scorpii. In Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् it is considered as benefic. Persons born under this will be good, compassionate, soft spoken and happy. The day on which the मोओन् is associated with this नक्षत्र is considered as auspicious for religious rites and good undertakings.
See also NAKṢATRA.

anukramaṇī
(‘coming in order’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस्, the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, grew in volume in course of time to such a proportion that it became very difficult to retain them in memory. Realizing this, sages like शौनक and कात्यायन composed special works which gave tables of contents of the वेदस् as also index of hymns and words. Such works are called ‘anukramaṇī’ or ‘anu-kramaṇikā.’ They usually give the first words of Vedic hymns, names of ṛṣis (sages) and छन्दस् (metre) as also of the देवतास् (deities) arranged in the same manner as they occur in the originals.
Śaunaka is said to have written ten such works on the Ṛgveda, like Ārṣānu-kramaṇī, Chando’nukramaṇī and Deva-tānukramaṇī. The famous Bṛhaddevatā is included in this series.
The अनुक्रमणी literature pertaining to the Ṛgveda has been greatly enriched by the Sarvānukramaṇī of another sage कात्यायन. This is an excellent compendium of all indices in one place. कात्यायन is reputed to have written an अनुक्रमणी on the Śukla Yajurveda also. अत्रि and Cārāyāṇa have authored two independent anukramaṇīs on the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
Sāmaveda has two anukramaṇīs: Ārṣa and Daivata.
The अनुक्रमणी literature of the Atharvaveda is called ‘pariśiṣṭa’ (appendix). Of the 70 pariśiṣṭas known to exist, Caraṇavyūha, the 49th, is the most celebrated.
All these works are mostly written in either the śloka (metrical, verse) or the sūtra (aphorism) style.
See also BṚHAD-DEVATĀ.
